The best local answer to the malaise of blockbuster season, BAMcinemaFest offers New Yorkers a chance to survey the glories and limitations of American independent cinema. Each year, the program at the Brooklyn Academy of Music (which starts its eighth iteration on Wednesday) plucks promising features and documentaries from Sundance, South by Southwest and elsewhere, and arranges them into a bouquet of puzzles, provocations and delights. The unevenness of the offerings is part of the festivalâ€™s appeal, and so is a palpable but hard-to-define consistency of themes, methods and attitudes.The dominant style might be described as an observant, cautious realism, an interest in small-scale stories shot in expressive, shallow-focus, closeup-heavy digital video and inflected a few degrees toward comedy, drama or even horror. Those generic distinctions are not always terribly important. â€œLittle Sister,â€ Zach Clarkâ€™s sweet-and-sad tale of a young nun and her family, could be classified as a comedy, since it sometimes takes a gently mocking view of its characters and situations. But the opening-night film, â€œLittle Men,â€ Ira Sachsâ€™s latest investigation of love and real estate in millennial New York, is probably a bit too melancholy to qualify. (Todd Solondzâ€™s â€œWiener-Dog,â€ the festival centerpiece, is a Todd Solondz movie, which is a genre unto itself. It opens commercially next week, so Iâ€™ll deal with it then. Werner Herzogâ€™s new documentary, â€œLo and Behold, Reveries of the Connected World,â€ is also, as you would expect, beyond category.)It can only be a coincidence that Mr. Sachs and Mr. Clark emphasize smallness in their titles, but itâ€™s also a statement of aesthetic principle. Both films are partly family portraits that try, without political posturing, to understand how social and political forces affect individuals. â€œLittle Menâ€ is mostly concerned with the friendship between two early-adolescent boys, Tony (Michael Barbieri) and Jake (Theo Taplitz), who meet in a rapidly changing Brooklyn neighborhood. Jake moves from Manhattan with his parents, an actor (Greg Kinnear) and a psychotherapist (Jennifer Ehle). Jakeâ€™s father has inherited the building where Tonyâ€™s mother (Paulina GarcÃ­a) has a dress shop. Though â€œgentrificationâ€ is never uttered, economic imperatives and parental stubbornness threaten the bond between the boys, an affection that carries a delicate, intriguing hint of sexual interest.â€œLittle Menâ€ was filmed in Brooklyn, on streets that audience members may recognize. Not every movie unfolds quite so close to home, but there is a clear pattern of filmmakers exploring nearby and familiar landscapes and people, often in search of shadows and hidden implications. Sometimes these are horrifyingly topical. Two films â€” Tim Suttonâ€™s â€œDark Night,â€ an inspired-by-facts fictional feature, and Kim A. Snyderâ€™s â€œNewtown,â€ a straightforward documentary â€” deal with recent mass shootings, and they are sure to be even more painful and grimly relevant after the massacre in Orlando, Fla., last weekend.â€œLittle Sisterâ€ handles volatile material â€” the effects of war, cultural and military, on young Americans â€” with a lighter touch. Anchored in Addison Timlinâ€™s low-key, sensitive performance, it takes place in the waning days of the George W. Bush administration. Colleen (Ms. Timlin) has moved from Asheville, N.C., to New York, but unlike other young migrants to the city, she has come to join a religious order. She returns home to see her brother, a badly injured veteran of the Iraq war, and finds herself in a muted sitcom universe streaked with pain and unspoken conflict. The movie suggests that some kind of reconciliation might be possible in this deeply divided country, in a way that is funny, disarmingly sincere and forgivably naÃ¯ve.The young hero of â€œMorris From America,â€ a 13-year-old African-American boy (the amazing Markees Christmas) living with his father (Craig Robinson) in Heidelberg, Germany, struggles with his own naÃ¯vetÃ©, and also with a form of racism that comes wreathed in smiles and Teutonic condescension. Itâ€™s not hard to imagine Morris hanging out with Tony and Jake in â€œLittle Men,â€ and this movie, directed by Chad Hartigan, is, like Mr. Sachsâ€™s, a coming-of-age-story told from an unusual angle. Itâ€™s sweet and sharp and very funny, with a precise sense of the stakes, the risks and the thrills that Morris encounters as he navigates his strange surroundings and the equally disruptive stirrings of his own dreams and desires.CinemaFest is, like most such events, intended as a showcase for directors. Modern film festivals, for better or worse, are bastions of auteurism. But they are also enlivened â€” in some cases you might say redeemed â€” by performers, and this yearâ€™s BAM program is, if anything, more revealing about the state of screen acting than about the directorâ€™s craft. Most films live comfortably within conventions of structure and visual texture, and directors with the nerve or talent to break out of them are rare in all corners of the movie industry. But actors often nowadays seem to have more freedom to push the boundaries of their art and to explore its radical possibilities.This is what Maggie Siff does in Elisabeth Subrinâ€™s â€œA Woman, a Part,â€ a psychological study of just how contradictory and terrifying it can be to pretend, as a matter of professional duty, to be someone else. The busy story, which winds in and out of the personal lives of its characters, is overshadowed by the haunted and haunting intensity that Ms. Siff and Cara Seymour, playing actresses with very different temperaments and biographies, bring to their roles and the roles within those roles.â€œA Woman, a Partâ€ finds an ideal companion piece in Robert Greeneâ€™s â€œKate Plays Christine,â€ a documentary that follows the actress Kate Lyn Sheil, a fixture of recent indie film, as she researches the role of Christine Chubbuck, a Florida television host whose on-air suicide in 1974 has become something of a media legend. Like Mr. Greeneâ€™s â€œActress,â€ â€œKate Plays Christineâ€ is a work of empathetic voyeurism, an at times uneasy collaboration between an unseen filmmaker and an exposed, self-conscious subject. Much of it is matter-of-fact almost to the point of banality â€” Ms. Sheil studies her characterâ€™s life and tries to approximate her looks and personality, as any serious actor would â€” but there is an almost superstitious undercurrent of menace running through the movie. Taking pictures and making up stories is a dangerous business.

Six Hours of Increased Memory By Adding This to BreakfastHeather Callaghan This substance can be added to scrambled egg recipes Can make porridge and oatmeal pop when something sweet is added. Researchers for the study published in the Asia Pacific Journal of Clinical Nutrition, found that adding just one gram (about 1/4 to 1/3 teaspoon) of turmeric to breakfast could help improve the memory of people who are in the very early stages of diabetes and at risk of cognitive impairment. Emeritus Professor Mark Wahlqvist said that early intervention by halting dementia/diabetes or softening its impact can reduce the burden of the aging populations rising cases of diabetes which leaves them predisposed to other disease and disorders. Wahlqvist recently led a study in Taiwan that tested the working memory of men and women aged 60 or older who had recently been diagnosed with untreated pre-diabetes. The New York City Council is urging Mayor Bill de Blasio to offer free lunch to all public school students, hire 1,000 more police officers and expand the summer job program for teenagers.These are three of the biggest-ticket items among $257 million in new spending that the Council has asked Mr. de Blasio to include in his May 8 executive budget. In his preliminary budget, the mayor proposed $73.7 billion for the fiscal year beginning July 1.Led by the cityâ€™s public advocate, Letitia James, supporters have been pushing since last fall for the city to eliminate all fees for school lunches, arguing that students who qualify for free lunch are often stigmatized by their classmates.Some 780,000 of the cityâ€™s 1.1 million public school students qualify for free or reduced-price lunch, but only 530,000 are currently enrolled in the program, supporters said.Students who testified before the Council in March described their peersâ€™ being mocked for lining up to get â€œfree-free,â€ as the program is derisively called. Supporters argue that making school lunch free for everyone would remove the stigma, and that children would no longer turn down the lunch to avoid ridicule.The Council estimated the added expense would be $20 million to $24 million, with the rest being covered by state and federal aid.When asked about the lunch proposal on Wednesday in Albany, Mr. de Blasio said that â€œthe goal is the right one.â€ But he added that it was a significant expenditure and could also have implications for the cityâ€™s receipt of federal education aid, some of which is based on the number of students in each school who qualify for free lunch.Speaker Melissa Mark-Viverito, who spoke at a news conference at City Hall announcing the Councilâ€™s budget proposal, said, â€œBureaucratic hurdles are not an excuse for letting children go hungry.â€Hiring an additional 1,000 police officers would cost $94.3 million, according to the Councilâ€™s budget estimates, but it would also help reduce the Police Departmentâ€™s overtime budget by $50 million.Ms. Mark-Viverito pointed to the nearly $600 million budgeted for police overtime as evidence that the department was being pushed beyond its capacity. â€œWe canâ€™t continue to overstretch our police force,â€ she said.Mr. de Blasio affirmed his thoughts that the cityâ€™s current force of 34,437 officers, down from 40,710 in 2001, is sufficient.â€œThe resources we have now are getting the job done,â€ he said. â€œAnd weâ€™re in a structural deficit. So I am not in the business of adding to that deficit when I believe we can get the job done with the resources and personnel we have now.â€Police Commissioner William J. Bratton has at times suggested that he disagreed. Last June, several months before his appointment, Mr. Bratton said that he thought the police force was too small. In December, when Mr. de Blasio announced he would name him as his commissioner, Mr. Bratton changed his tune, saying that he thought the size of the force was â€œadequate.â€The Council also recommends that the city increase spending on veterans by $1.4 million, expand antigun violence programs at a cost of $12 million, spend $1 million on four new technology incubators and increase the number of slots in the cityâ€™s six-week summer youth employment program for 14- to 24-year-olds, at a cost of $27.2 million. The fee would go into a fund to preserve and develop affordable housing.The Council would also like to reclassify so-called carried interest â€” the profits earned by many investment fund managers â€” as ordinary business income instead of investment income. In New York City, fund managers pay personal income tax on this compensation, but not unincorporated business tax.If passed, that change could bring some $200 million in new revenue, officials said. LONDON â€”  The Queen is dead. Charles, paranoid and power obsessed, dissolves Parliament and parks a tank outside Buckingham Palace. While Prince William dithers, his steely and pragmatic wife, Kate, orchestrates a palace coup to save the monarchy and prevent Britain from sliding into civil war.So goes the audacious plot of â€œKing Charles III,â€ a new play by Mike Bartlett, which opened here last week at the Almeida Theater to glowing, if somewhat scandalized, reviews. The critic for The New Statesman called it the â€œboldest and most provocative play about the royal family in British theatrical history,â€ adding, â€œIf the Lord Chamberlain still policed the stage, Bartlett would be in the Tower,â€ a reference to the royal official who had the power to censor plays until 1968.Advertisements for the play â€” showing the real Prince Charles dressed for his coronation â€” were barred from the London Underground until the image of the princeâ€™s face was heavily pixelated. Most advance tickets have already sold out, but more will be released on the day of each performance. â€œI suspect people will be camping out on the streets,â€ said a critic from The Telegraph. Written in iambic pentameter, modeled on Shakespearean histories like â€œRichard IIâ€ but set in the near future, the play explores what might happen if a British monarch bucked centuries of tradition and refused to rubber-stamp the will of Parliament. In the process, Mr. Bartlett imagines Queen Elizabethâ€™s funeral; Diana, Princess of Wales, as a ghost; and Prince Harry running off with a grungy art student he meets at the London nightclub Boujis. She takes him to Dans le Noir, a London restaurant where patrons eat in the dark, and there he is mistaken for a real estate agent. â€œWe talked about mortgages!â€ the happy prince says.Part fantasy, part comedy, â€œKing Charles IIIâ€ is still intended as a serious inquiry into the role the monarchy plays in Britain.â€œHere we have two things that are central to the DNA of this country: Shakespeare and the royal family,â€ said Rupert Goold, the playâ€™s director. â€œAs the play emerged in production, we realized more and more that this is our â€˜Godfather,â€™ this is our ur-family onto whom we map all our own families, and we need to treat them like stiff-upper-lip, rhetorical, ancient Corleones.â€The play is the first directed by Mr. Goold in his debut season as artistic director of the Almeida, a fashionable 325-seat theater in the Islington section of London. Mr. Gooldâ€™s earlier experiments have also been attention grabbing: turning â€œAmerican Psychoâ€ into a musical, for example, and directing Patrick Stewart in a bloody, Stalinist-era â€œMacbeth.â€ His provocative style would have normally made him resistant to a new play in verse, he said, adding that it is the type of thing written by â€œretired majors or strange little women in the home counties.â€Those labels hardly describe Mr. Bartlett, 33, one of the most successful young playwrights in Britain, whose daring, cutting-edge explorations â€” including â€œLove, Love, Love,â€ â€œBullâ€ and a play that The New York Times referred to as â€œThe Cockfight Playâ€ â€” have touched on everything from global warming to office politics to bisexuality.In an interview last week, Mr. Bartlett said he has always been fascinated by the complicated gravitational pull that the monarchy exerts on public and private life in Britain.â€œWhen Diana died, the response of the British people was so astonishing, and the same with William and Kateâ€™s wedding,â€ he said. â€œSuddenly, all these incredibly intelligent, very sophisticated people become deliberate peasants, and I donâ€™t mean that in a judgmental way. But thereâ€™s something about hierarchy thatâ€™s comforting. And thatâ€™s a very uncomfortable idea in 21st-century thought.â€The action of the play begins when Charles (Tim Pigott-Smith) withholds his signature from a privacy law passed by Parliament that would partly restrict freedom of the press because of past indiscretions, including phone hacking. Justifying his shocking decision to reassert royal power, Charles says that the British people possess a â€œwise and ancient bondâ€ with the crown thatâ€™s far stronger than their mere 500-year-old attachment to democracy, which he dismisses as â€œan option added on/ like SatNav on a car, it does not come/As standard.â€œMr. Pigott-Smith, who has appeared in dozens of Shakespeareâ€™s works â€” famously as Octavius in Peter Hallâ€™s 1987 staging of â€œAntony and Cleopatraâ€ at the National Theater â€” said this play would come as a special thrill for those schooled in Shakespeare. â€œIn the first scene, you meet the royal family, and in the second scene, you meet Prince Harry in a nightclub. Well, thatâ€™s straight out of Prince Hal in the tavern on Eastcheap,â€ he said, referring to â€œHenry IV, Part 1.â€Mr. Pigott-Smith, who has met Prince Charles several times, said he has â€œgreat respect for the monarchy,â€ and would not have taken the part if the play seemed frivolous. That concern was dispelled, he said, when he read the script, which he called â€œa staggering achievement.â€Mr. Bartlett said that the decision to set his play in the future was done to avoid the trap into which other portrayals of royal life have sometimes stumbled: romanticization. The play is one of several recent dramatic investigations of the royals on film (â€œDiana,â€ â€œThe Queenâ€) and onstage, including Peter Morganâ€™s â€œThe Audience,â€ which played here last year, and Moira Buffiniâ€™s â€œHandbagged,â€ a play about Queen Elizabethâ€™s relationship with Margaret Thatcher that is now at the Vaudeville Theater in the West End.â€œThereâ€™s a huge difference between dramatizing something in the past and this sort of future history thing,â€ Mr. Bartlett said. â€œBy looking to the future, you free up the audienceâ€™s preconceptions about the family, so the audience is not stuck in its ideas of what the royal family was. You have a freer hand to tell a new story.â€Mr. Bartlett and Mr. Goold both said they were surprised by the way Kate, the duchess of Cambridge, played by Lydia Wilson, was described by some critics as a â€œpoisonously ambitiousâ€ or â€œscheming.â€â€œSheâ€™s no more scheming than many of the men in the play,â€ Mr. Bartlett said. â€œBut when you have a woman whoâ€™s powerful and clever and not of royal birth in a play like this, everyone immediately says, â€˜Oh, itâ€™s Lady Macbeth.â€™Â â€œ At one point in the play, Kateâ€™s character comments on how sheâ€™s regarded as â€œjust a plastic dollâ€:Whose only job is prettying the Prince, and thenIf possible, get pregnant with the royalAnd noble bump, to there produce some heirs.Mr. Bartlett, an unapologetic populist, said that he wrote his play as much for London theatergoers as the readers of the British gossip magazine Hello.â€œItâ€™s written to be appealing to people who hate the royal family, love the royal family, young people who feel very disconnected from the old generation but who might know a bit more about Harry,â€ he said. â€œWe try to collect all those different pockets of audience and then pull them in toward the main thrust of the story, which is exactly what Shakespeare does. Thatâ€™s the tradition: Everybody is welcome.â€

The Baulkham Hills African Ladies Troupe begins with a close-up of a soulful-looking African woman in a pink singlet. Sheâ€™s in front of a blue projected background simulating rain, touching her face. Her eyes are closed and her hands are wet. Small streaks of water trickle down her arms as her voiceover begins: â€œI love my neck â€¦ â€ Whatever beauty that moment has turns devastating in a heartbeat. As a deep, slow, operatic song plays on the soundtrack, matched to images of other womenâ€™s faces and hands, the narrator completes her sentence: â€œbecause it was never touched.â€  Director Ros Horinâ€™s documentary is a behind-the-scenes account of the titular stage production and the remarkable people at its core. Arriving in cinemas this week after making the rounds at the Sydney and Melbourne film festivals, the filmâ€™s champions include veteran film-makers Gillian Armstrong (â€œemotional and upliftingâ€) and George Miller (â€œremarkable and unforgettableâ€).     Ros Horin, the director of The Baulkham Hills African Ladies Troupe.   Horin, an experienced stage director, worked with four African-raised women to turn their harrowing lives into a cathartic experience. First as theatre and now as a film she hopes will have a long life.  Rosemary grew up in Kenya and was abused for several years by members of her own family. Aminata was 16 when she was kidnapped by a rebel leader during the Sierra Leone civil war in the 1990s. She became a sex slave. Yarrie, a victim of the same war, grew up in a refugee camp in Guinea. Thereâ€™s also Yordanos, whose story we will illuminate in a moment.  After introducing the four key subjects â€“ none of whom had professional acting experience â€“ Horinâ€™s documentary poses a question she has spent a lot of time contemplating: how do women survive something like this?  â€œI have arrived at the conclusion that you can survive and reconstruct your life but it is absolutely dependent on breaking your silence,â€ she tells Guardian Australia. â€œBeing able tell your story and have it acknowledged and heard and validated.  â€œJust imagine having this deep dark secret inside you that you feel you canâ€™t mention to anyone. Itâ€™s like having a rock inside your stomach. Like this thing thatâ€™s constantly pulling you down.â€ Yordanosâ€™ journey to regain her life involved combining the theatre production with ongoing weekly counselling. When she was a young child, she watched her father kill her mother. When she was five years old, she was taken and trained to be a child soldier by the Eritrean army. For a decade and a half she suffered violence and sexual abuse.  Preparing the play required extensively workshopping sessions to find ways to tell each personâ€™s stories. This meant Yordanos and the rest of the group had to revisit the trauma of their pasts, session after session, week after week. All this before getting on stage and reliving it, again and again, in front of strangers. It became too much for her. Four weeks in, Yordanos suffered an emotional collapse and quit.  â€œI felt tired and drained and I couldnâ€™t continue,â€ she says. â€œThereâ€™s so many things that happened. I was five when I was kidnapped. From that age until my teenage life, I was in that place. While making this I had so many flashbacks and I couldnâ€™t cope with all of that.  â€œI felt like the best thing for me was to withdraw. Just, get away from me, I donâ€™t want to be telling this again. But my counsellor thought I was strong enough to go back and continue it. That is what I did. I was so grateful I got to finish it.  â€œIn my life I have been voiceless. But to stand there and speak in such a way, to say â€˜this is what happened to me and Iâ€™m explaining itâ€™, I think it has huge power.â€    Yordanos Haile-Michael was a young child when she watched her father kill her mother. At the age of five, she was taken and trained to be a child soldier in the Eritrean army. Photograph: Goodship   In the early days of workshopping, Horin, concerned about the womenâ€™s welfare, would sometimes float the idea of abandoning the play altogether when things became overwhelming. These conversations tended to be marked by long stretches of silence, she says, eventually broken by â€œone voice which would pipe up and say, â€˜Yes, this pain is coming out. But I canâ€™t tell you how much better I feel.â€™â€  The director used various techniques to protect the women from revisiting the most painful aspects of their stories. Instead of Aminata reading out a court testimony detailing her rape, for example, Horin swapped roles, so Aminata became the lawyer character and a friend played her. This sort of approach was used with each of the women in various ways, including through video footage and songs.  â€œIf somebody was very fragile and they were observing aspects of their story I could say to them, â€˜Tonight you donâ€™t have to come on stage and observe that or even listen to it,â€™â€ Horin says. â€œThere wasnâ€™t just one structure to the play. There was a kind of A version, then a B version, then a C version. This was all invented out of necessity. How to solve a practical problem and not be too hard on the women.â€ The results are inspiring to say the least. The group bonded and grew like a family; they now refer to each other as sisters. There are scenes in the film that bring tears to your eyes, though the story is ultimately life-affirming. Among its messages, perhaps, is that hope comes in many forms.    â€˜Among its messages is that hope comes in many formsâ€™: Yordanos Haile-Michael, Rosemary Kariuki-Fyfe and Yarrie Bangura. Photograph: Goodship   The four subjects found different pathways to resilience. One has focused on poetry, another on participating in philanthropic projects. Yordanos says that because of sticking with the stage production â€“ slogging it out when her instincts told her to quit â€“ she is now in a better place than ever. â€œI tried so hard to fit in with my own community, it didnâ€™t work,â€ she says. â€œBut this has given me faith in humans. I made friends from different backgrounds and I get to be seen as totally the person I am. I came to accept that this is what I am meant to be and I am OK with that person.  â€œFor someone like me, I have no one to blame. I canâ€™t go out there saying, â€˜You have done this to me.â€™ There is no one to say sorry, or even to acknowledge me as a human being. The play, for people to come to see it, to meet so many different people and to be able to talk about it openly â€“ itâ€™s amazing. To me, I got my life back. I got me back.â€  â€¢ The Baulkham Hills African Ladies Troupe is in cinemas now

Less than three miles from the organized bustle and cheer of Walt Disney World, the community of Celebration has been a glass figurine on a shelf -- a place to be admired from afar but reserved for a rarefied few. The Disney-designed suburb, as quiet as the theme park is busy, is a perfect postcard of palm-tree-lined streets, 1990s architecture and 1950s family-friendly ambiance. But if Disney World is the place where dreams come true, Celebration has been a distant fantasy for many would-be residents, a community where houses often sold for $1 million or more. 'It's a little place where people come to get away from everything,' said Mike Pieper, an Osceola County sheriff's deputy who patrols the streets here. 'It's a place you dream about living.' Specifically, it's a place (ital) he (end ital) dreams about living. 'Absolutely,' Pieper said. 'If I wasn't on a government salary.' In Celebration, he said, the biggest crime problems are parking violations and stolen bikes. Now, for the first time, just maybe, he and others on modest incomes can live that dream. The recession has closed many doors, but it has also cracked open the intangible gates surrounding desirable neighborhoods such as Celebration. Falling house prices have allowed some families to buy into a quality of life they likely couldn't have afforded otherwise, a community that offers Fourth of July fireworks and a Christmas supply of fake snow. 'If you would have asked us in the last five years, `What's the least expensive home you have?,' ' said Sonny Buoncervello, who owns Hometown Realty in Celebration, 'our answer was always, `Our houses start at $400,000, they average $600,000 to $700,000 and you have some up into the millions.' 'Today, I could take you to a single-family house selling for $270,000 or $280,000,' he said. He is standing in a five-bedroom house that was once valued at more than $1 million and is now available for $745,000. There was no foreclosure sign outside -- only a quaint 'Home Available,' the generic notice placed outside for-sale houses here, regardless of how the property hit the market. A hole in the kitchen wall revealed this house was not surrendered by choice. A movie projector was once mounted there, but the last owners took it with them as a way to salvage something, said Donna McGrath, the real estate agent showing the house that day and, like Buoncervello, one of the first residents to move into Celebration. Their daughters grew up together, walking along streets at night, unafraid because they knew everyone who lived along their route. This is a place where, true to the Disney fantasy of small-town America, there's a lemonade party when someone new moves in. 'This is definitely a relationship community,' said Buoncervello, the town's unofficial mayor, a title that adorns the license plate on his electric car, who has lived here 13 years. When children misbehave, parents call to apologize, Buoncervello said. At his previous home three miles away, his daughter was allowed to stay overnight at three houses; within six months in Celebration, he gave her permission to stay at more than 50. He and other real estate agents have watched as the recession has relaxed a once-tight market. Where a lottery system was once needed to determine who would get a chance to move in, now about 10 percent of Celebration's single-family houses are on the market. The upside is that 'you've got people who never thought they could live here, now coming over here to see the possibilities,' McGrath said. 'It's so unusual for a community like this to have this situation. For most people, this was a dream. ... It wasn't an investment.' The downside: 'You'll see a house that you know people planned on using for the rest of their lives and they just had to walk away,' Buoncervello added. Take the house that a Louisiana builder bought, lived in for 11 nights with his family and then was forced to put up for sale, complete with furniture and the BMW in the garage. 'Everything stays, the electronics, everything,' Buoncervello said. 'Everything stays, except their personal pictures.' The asking price for the house is $749,500, with owner financing available. Already, offers have been made. Most houses, especially those under $400,000, don't linger long, said Kathy Yeasted, an agent at Imagination Realty on Celebration Avenue. 'We have people walking in every day.' Unlike other communities left in a state of mid-construction by the recession, every amenity that was planned in Celebration has been finished since it opened in 1996. There's a movie theater, a church, a golf course and a school. On the same day that Buoncervello and McGrath held the open house, Lynda and John Kangas pulled into a driveway of a nearby 'available' house, with Lynda's sister and niece. 'Sight-dreaming,' Lynda Kangas said. 'We're definitely sight-dreaming.' The couple live about 10 miles away in an RV park that suited their dream of traveling the country. Later, they drove to the house McGrath and Buoncervello had shown earlier. Now the doors were locked, so the family settled on peeking through the windows. 'Oh my goodness, look at that -- it's so beautiful,' Lynda Kangas said, turning to her niece. 'Go tell Johnny he doesn't have to remarry me for our 50th anniversary, just buy me this.'
